lesson.title: The Morning Round
lesson.subtitle: se lever, se laver, s'habiller, se coucher — chaining daily routine verbs.

hook.title: Chaining the Morning and Evening Routine — and Body Parts
hook.content: Walk through your day with se lever ('get up'), se laver ('wash'), s'habiller ('get dressed'), and se coucher ('go to bed'). When you wash your hands, the reflexive pronoun me already tells whose hands they are, so French uses the definite article les instead of 'my': Je me lave les mains! And in the past tense, ALL reflexive verbs live inside the être house: Je me suis levé(e)!

footnotes.title: Why reflexives live inside the être house in the past tense!
footnotes.content: Every reflexive verb forms its passé composé with être: Je me suis levé ('I got up'), Elle s'est habillée ('She got dressed')!

pattern.title: Present: Je me lève; Past: Je me suis levé(e); Body Parts: Je me lave les mains
pattern.content: Chain routine verbs across present and past.
pattern.linguist_note: Inalienable possession of body parts in French uses a reflexive dative clitic + definite article.
pattern.trap_note: Don't say *Je me lave mes mains or *J'ai me levé — use les mains, and use être in the past (Je me suis levé)!

exercises.prompt: Match each routine sentence with its English meaning:

matching_pairs.english: Je me lève à sept heures
matching_pairs.german: I get up at seven o'clock

matching_pairs.english: Je me lave les mains (definite les!)
Je me suis levé tôt (être in past!)

exercises.target_answer: I get up at seven o'clock, I wash my hands, I get dressed quickly, I go to bed late, I got up early
exercises.meaning: Je me lève à sept heures, Je me lave les mains (definite les!), Je m'habille vite, Je me couche tard, Je me suis levé tôt (être in past!)
exercises.explanation: Reflexives use definite articles with body parts and take être in the passé composé.

exercises.prompt: What is the literal word-for-word structure of 'Je me lave les mains'?
exercises.meaning: Literal structure: I to-myself wash the hands
exercises.explanation: me ('to-myself') already marks the owner, so French uses les mains ('the hands').

exercises.prompt: How do you say 'I got up at eight o'clock' in the passé composé?
options: Je me suis levé à huit heures
Je m'ai levé à huit heures
J'ai me levé à huit heures
exercises.target_answer: Je me suis levé à huit heures
exercises.meaning: I got up at eight o'clock
exercises.explanation: All reflexive verbs take être in the passé composé: Je me suis levé(e)!

exercises.idea: I get up and I get dressed quickly
cues: I get up → Je me lève
and I get dressed quickly → et je m'habille rapidement
idea_parts: second reflexive + adverb → et je m'habille rapidement
exercises.target_answer: Je me lève et je m'habille rapidement
exercises.meaning: I get up and get dressed quickly
exercises.explanation: Repeat je + reflexive pronoun on each verb: Je me lève et je m'habille.

exercises.prompt: Listen and write the whole sentence.
exercises.spoken: Elle s'est levée tôt ce matin
exercises.target_answer: Elle s'est levée tôt ce matin
exercises.meaning: She got up early this morning
exercises.explanation: se + est elides to s'est, and levée agrees with Elle.
exercises.affirmation: You wrote Elle s'est levée with the feminine -e!

summary.outcome: Chain reflexive daily-routine verbs across present and passé composé (with être), and use definite articles with body parts.

use_example.german: Ce matin, je me suis levé tôt et je me suis habillé.
use_example.english: This morning, I got up early and got dressed.

summary.takeaway: All reflexives take être in the past (Je me suis levé), and body parts take le/la/les (Je me lave les mains).
summary.curiosity_teaser: Up next on Le Pont ([25] il y a): see how The Morning Round leads directly into il y a.

twist.prompt: Think it through again without looking back — express "I get up and get dressed quickly" in French:
twist.target_answer: Je me lève et je m'habille rapidement
twist.explanation: Re-constructing "Je me lève et je m'habille rapidement" from the underlying rule cements the pattern of The Morning Round.

lever.context_phrase: Je me lève à sept heures.
lever.etymology_derivation: Latin levāre 'to lift' — lever, levitate, elevate. se lever: you raise yourself.

laver.english_meaning: to wash (se laver: to wash oneself)
laver.etymology_derivation: Notice French uses the reflexive + definite article for body parts: je me lave les mains.

coucher.english_meaning: to lay down; to put to bed
coucher.etymology_derivation: collocāre 'to place together' → couch — the furniture is the verb, frozen.

me.etymology_derivation: Elides to m' before a vowel: il m'écoute.

te.etymology_derivation: Elides to t' before a vowel: je t'aime.

tête.etymology_derivation: Latin testa 'terracotta pot' — Roman slang for the skull! The circumflex marks the vanished s.

heure.etymology_derivation: Latin hōra. Silent H triggers elision: l'heure.

ion.name: The -ION Bridge
ion.phonetic_rule: Spelling converts 1:1; the final N is nasalised — thought, not said (collection /kɔlɛksjɔ̃/).
ion.historical_linguistics: English absorbed thousands of Latin-dress nouns through Norman French and later Renaissance borrowing. The -tion/-sion endings are the single largest cognate landing zone between the two languages.
ion.philological_note: Every -ION noun is feminine, so the article is la — elided to l' before a vowel. The ending is a gender decoder, not a memory item.
ion.literature_source: Walter, Le français dans tous les sens (1988); Pope, From Latin to Modern French (1952).

ation.name: The -ation Engine
ation.historical_linguistics: French -er verbs descend from Latin -āre; the English -ation nouns and French verbs are two leaves of the same Latin branch, so the noun unlocks the verb with almost no loss.
ation.philological_note: The whole -ation goes — célébration → célébrer, never *célébrater. Test for the -ation noun in English first; it is the proof the verb converts.
ation.literature_source: Guillaume, Temps et verbe (1929); standard French morphophonology.

ite.name: The -ité Bridge
ite.phonetic_rule: English final -ity becomes stressed final -ité /ite/ — the é marks the syllable English swallows.
ite.historical_linguistics: Latin -itās survives in English -ity and French -ité; both are bookish layers grafted onto the everyday vocabulary, which is why they convert with no sound loss.
ite.philological_note: All -ité nouns are feminine (la possibilité, la liberté).
ite.literature_source: Pope (1952); Brunot, Histoire de la langue française.

ance.name: The -ance/-ence Twins
ance.phonetic_rule: Same spelling family; the AN is nasal: différence /difeʁɑ̃s/.
ance.historical_linguistics: Latin -antia/-entia produced English -ance/-ence and French -ance/-ence directly; the pair is one of the highest-conversion zones in the vocabulary.

e.name: The é/ed Twins
e.phonetic_rule: The past participle in -é /e/ is the English -ed: mangé/manged, décidé/decided, marié/married.
e.historical_linguistics: The Norman conquest put French participles straight into English verb morphology — countless English past tenses ARE French participles wearing English spelling.
e.philological_note: With avoir, the participle never agrees; with être (motion verbs), it does — the one agreement the past asks for.
e.literature_source: Baugh & Cable, A History of the English Language (2002).

ment.name: The -ment Adverb Bridge
ment.phonetic_rule: English -ly adverbs convert to -ment: exactement, rapidement — the ME is nasal, like pain.
ment.historical_linguistics: Latin -mente ('in a ... mind') became French -ment and English kept the same suffix for nouns (moment, comment) — but French built adverbs with it where English built them with -ly.
ment.philological_note: Feminine adjectives get an -e before -ment: exacte → exactement.

eur.name: The -eur Bridge
eur.phonetic_rule: Latin -or/-er nouns convert to -eur /œʁ/: doctor → docteur, color → couleur.
eur.historical_linguistics: The agent and quality suffixes of Latin split three ways in English (-or, -er, -our) but re-merge in French as -eur.
eur.philological_note: -eur is usually masculine — couleur and erreur are the famous rebels. The lesson names the exceptions before you trust the rule blindly.

able.name: The -able Bridge
able.phonetic_rule: Adjectives in -able/-ible convert as-is: adorable, possible, invisible — only the stress moves.
able.historical_linguistics: Latin -ābilis/-ibilis landed in both languages with the spelling intact; it is the highest-fidelity conversion family in the whole bridge.
able.philological_note: Same form, different stress: invisible with the beat on the final syllable in French.

doublet.name: Norman Doublets
doublet.phonetic_rule: Same Latin word entered English twice — once Germanic-dressed, once Norman: warden/gardien, estate/état, hôtel/hospital.
doublet.historical_linguistics: After 1066 English borrowed Norman French wholesale; centuries of independent drift mean many English words have a French twin that looks different and sounds different but is the same word.
doublet.philological_note: French dropped Latin H everywhere (hôtel, homme) and dropped S before consonants (état, école) — the dropped letters are the fingerprints.
